result.title: Spatial assessment of PM<sub>2.5</sub> exposure and health risks in Upper Northern Thailand: Implications for public health.

result.abstractText: Upper Northern Thailand experiences recurrent seasonal PM<sub>2.5</sub> pollution, particularly during periods of biomass burning. This study assessed the spatial and seasonal distribution of ambient PM<sub>2.5</sub> concentrations and health risks across eight provinces during 2021-2023. Non-carcinogenic risk was evaluated using hazard quotients (HQs) relative to PM<sub>2.5</sub> benchmarks established by the World Health Organization (WHO), the U.S. National Ambient Air Quality Standards (U.S. NAAQS), and Thailand's National Environment Board (NEB) standards. The regional mean (± SD) PM<sub>2.5</sub> concentration was 27.57 ± 23.40 µg/m<sup>3</sup> (range, 8.40-78.64 µg/m<sup>3</sup>). Mean HQs were higher in the dry season than in the rainy season, increasing from 1.19 ± 0.23-4.31 ± 1.22 for WHO guidelines, from 0.50 ± 0.10-1.80 ± 0.51 for U.S. NAAQS, and from 0.24 ± 0.05-0.86 ± 0.24 for NEB standards. The PM<sub>2.5</sub> concentrations and HQs varied greatly among provinces and seasons, with the highest values in the dry season. The results show that there are large differences in space and time of PM<sub>2.5</sub> exposure in Upper Northern Thailand, and the dry season is the time of greatest exposure. Spatially resolved assessment of PM<sub>2.5</sub> can help identify areas and periods requiring closer air-quality surveillance and targeted exposure-reduction measures.
